label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**The house in Glenmore**

Hello to all of you, in Boston and Perth and Leeds and wherever else this reaches.

I've started this post three times now and torn it up twice, which Úna will tell you is about my usual rate. I'm going to try to just say it plainly and then explain myself, because a good few of you already know the main part of it, and you didn't hear it from me. That's on me and I'll come back to it.

So here it is. I've agreed a sale on the house in Glenmore, the old Mulkerrin place outside Oughterard where Tom grew up. The sale was agreed on the 3rd of November and it closes on the 15th of January 2027. I'm putting the date down in black and white so that nobody has to hear it from somebody else at a wedding or on a WhatsApp. That's the date. After that the house belongs to someone else.

I know that's a hard thing to read, for some of you more than others. It was a hard thing to sign.

**How you found out**

I'll start with the bit I got wrong, because it would be dishonest to skip over it.

I meant to tell everyone properly. I had it in my head that I'd ring Declan first, then write something here, and do it all in the one week so it would be fair. But I told a few people locally while I was still getting used to the idea myself, because when you live in a place people ask, and you can't always say "nothing new" with a straight face. It got around, the way things do. Declan heard it from his cousin Gráinne on a WhatsApp message before he heard it from his own mother.

I'm sorry for that. I'm sorry to Declan most of all, and to anyone else who found out in bits and pieces and felt they'd been left out of something that matters to them. You weren't wrong to feel that. I should have picked up the phone sooner and I didn't, and I can't undo it now. So this is me saying it once, to everyone, the whole of it, so there's nothing else going round.

I want to be clear about one thing, though, so nobody is confused. I'm sorry for how you found out. I'm not sorry for the decision. I've thought about it for a long time and I'd make it again. I'll try to explain why.

**The house**

For those of the younger ones who were never out there, or only went once as a small child and remember nothing but the midges, here is the house.

Tom's grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin, built it in 1931. It sits up above the lake with the haggard behind it and the land running down towards the water. Pádraig built it to last and it did last, nearly a hundred years, which is more than most of what gets built now. Three generations of Mulkerrins lived in it or came back to it, and then us, for every summer and Christmas and half the bank holidays in between.

When Tom died in March of 2024 I couldn't think about it at all. I just kept it going. Every fortnight since, I've driven out from Galway, forty minutes there and forty back, to open the windows and air the place, run the taps, check the pipes hadn't burst, make sure no slates had come off in the last storm. I'd have a cup of tea standing up in the kitchen because it was too cold to sit, and I'd lock up and drive home again. I won't pretend it was all a burden. Some days I liked it. Some days I'd sit in the car at the gate for ten minutes before I could make myself go in. Mostly it was just a job that had to be done, and nobody else was there to do it.

In September I had Ó Flaithearta's out to look at the roof, because I could see daylight in the back bedroom where there shouldn't be any. They came back with a quote of €38,000 for the slates and the back chimney. That's before the damp in the back bedroom, which has got a lot worse in the last two winters. On top of that the septic tank has to be replaced, and that has to be done no matter who buys it, so it was never a question of whether.

I'm a retired primary teacher. I don't have €38,000 sitting in a drawer, and even if I did, fixing the roof wouldn't fix the fact that the house needs someone living in it. A house that's only visited goes downhill. You can air it every fortnight for a hundred years and it'll still be a house nobody lives in.

**The part I haven't told anyone**

Last February, on one of my fortnightly trips, there was frost on the step at the back door and I slipped on it. I went down hard. I lay there for about twenty minutes before I could get myself up. There was nobody around, you know yourselves how far it is from the nearest house, and my phone was in my bag in the car.

I didn't break anything, thank God. I was bruised black and blue down one side for a month and I told people I'd walked into the press door. I didn't tell anyone what really happened. Not the doctor, not Úna, not Declan. I'm telling you all now because it's part of the honest version of this and I said I'd give you that.

I won't dress it up. Since then I've been afraid out there on my own. I'd never been afraid in that house in my life. I'd stand at the back door now and look at the step and think about it. In the winter it gets dark by half four, and I'd be rushing to get finished and out before the light went, and that's no way to be in a place you love. I'm seventy-one. I'm in decent health, but I'm not getting any younger, and I can't keep driving out on frosty mornings to a house with no one in it, hoping I don't end up on the ground again with nobody to know.

So that's the plain reason, really. I can't maintain it and I'm afraid of being alone there. Those two things together. The rest is just the reasons that made it possible to accept.

**Who's buying it**

The couple buying it are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, so he's not a stranger to the area, and they have two small children. They want to live in it. It's going to be their home, not a holiday let and not something to do up and sell on.

I'll tell you something else, because I'd rather you heard it from me than wondered about it. Over the summer there was a higher offer from a couple in Dublin. A good bit higher. They were perfectly nice people, but it was very clear it would be a weekend place, maybe rented out the rest of the time. I took the Joyces' offer instead, on purpose. The price is fair. It's not a giveaway and I'm not a saint, I'm not going to go short. But I took less because I wanted a family in it.

Tom always said that house should have children in it. He said it more times than I can count, usually when one of you lot was tearing round the place or falling into the lake. He'd say it should never be turned into a museum. When I sat at the table with Aoife and Kevin and their two small ones, the little lad running in and out the door the whole time, I kept hearing Tom saying it. I'm fairly sure he'd have approved. I know not everyone will see it that way, but that's what I believe.

**What we're keeping**

I know for some of you the worry is that everything will just be gone. It won't be. These are coming with us:

The dresser is going to Úna's. It's been in that kitchen since before any of us were born and it deserves to stay in the family and be used, not stored.

Pádraig's fiddle. I haven't decided yet who should have it long-term, and I'd like to talk to a few of you about that rather than just decide it myself, given how the rest of this has gone.

All the photographs. Every box of them, including the ones in the back of the wardrobe that nobody's looked at since the eighties. If anyone wants to help me go through them and get some of them copied for the families abroad, I'd be glad of it.

The Sacred Heart lamp. I'm not going to leave that behind, and I don't think Tom's mother would forgive me if I did.

The gate sign. That's coming with us too.

The Joyces have also said, and I didn't ask them, they offered, that any of the family can come out and walk the land any time. Down to the lake, up past the haggard, wherever you like. I think they meant it. I think they understand what they're buying a bit better than a lot of people would.

**What I'll remember**

I don't want this whole post to be about roofs and septic tanks, so let me say a bit about what that house was.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was lashing rain, and the cattle were standing along the wall watching the whole thing like a jury. He'd planned something nicer, I found out afterwards, but the weather didn't cooperate and he lost his nerve waiting for it to clear, so he just asked me there in the muck. I said yes before he'd finished the question. I've told that story so many times the grandchildren roll their eyes, but I'm putting it here anyway.

All the children learned to swim in the lake below the house. Freezing, every one of them, I don't care what month it was. Declan was the worst for it, or the best, depending on how you look at it. He would not come out. You'd be standing on the bank with the towel calling him, and he'd be out there with his lips gone blue, teeth chattering, telling you he wasn't cold. Tom used to say he'd make a great Mulkerrin, too stubborn to know when he was beaten. I think about that a lot lately.

There are a hundred other things. Christmases with the range going and all of us squashed into that kitchen. The smell of the turf. Tom and his brothers arguing about hurling at the table. The year the cow got into the garden. You'll all have your own, and I hope you'll keep them, and tell them to your own children.

**What I've come to understand**

This is the part I find hardest to put into words, so bear with me.

When Tom died, the house felt like the last bit of him that was still there. His coat was still on the hook. His boots were by the back door. Driving out there every fortnight was a way of keeping hold of him, I think, even though I wouldn't have said that at the time. I was afraid that if I let go of the house I'd be letting go of him, and I wasn't ready for that. I don't think I could have sold it in the first year. I'm not sure I could have sold it last year.

But over the best part of two years I've slowly come round to something. I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. He isn't in the slates or the back chimney. He's in all of you. He's in the stories, and the fiddle, and the photographs, and the way Declan holds his shoulders, and the way the grandchildren laugh. Keeping a cold empty house from falling down isn't the same as keeping him. Some weeks, standing in that kitchen with my coat on, it felt like the opposite. It felt like I was keeping a place where he wasn't.

I don't expect everyone to feel the same, and I'm not asking you to. I'm just telling you where I've got to, so you understand it wasn't done lightly, or quickly, or for the money.

**To Declan**

Declan, I know you read these, so I'm going to say this here as well as on the phone.

When you rang me at two in the morning your time, you were upset, and you'd every right to be. You'd found out from Gráinne on a WhatsApp, and that should never have happened. You said I was selling Dad. I said things back to you that I shouldn't have said, and I've been sorry about that every day since. I was tired and I was hurt and I took it out on you. That wasn't fair.

I should have talked to you before I made the decision, not after. I regret that. I really do. But I'm not going to pretend I'd have waited, because I wouldn't. I couldn't have waited until your visit next summer. I couldn't face another winter of it, not after the fall. I know that's hard to hear, and I'm sorry it's hard, but it's the truth and you'd know if I was lying to you anyway. You always did.

I'm not angry with you. I want you to know that more than anything else in this post. I'm not angry, and I'm not waiting for you to say sorry first, or at all. The door's open. Ring me any time, whatever time it is there, and we'll talk about it properly, or we'll talk about something else entirely if that's easier. Whenever you're ready. I'll be here.

And for what it's worth, I don't think I'm selling your father. I think he'd be glad of the Joyce children in the lake. I think he'd have told me to do it a year ago.

**The day out**

Before the house is cleared, I'd like us to have one more day out there together. Anyone who can make it.

**Sunday the 13th of December**, at the house in Glenmore. I'll do soup and sandwiches, and if anyone wants to bring something else, you'd be very welcome, but you don't have to. Bring wellies, because the field down to the lake will be a swamp, it always is in December. Bring the children. Bring anyone who has a memory of the place.

I'd like us to walk the land, go down to the lake (no swimming, Declan), stand in the haggard for a minute, and have a cup of tea in the kitchen with the range lit one last time. If anyone wants to take a few photographs, or bring the fiddle out and give it an airing, or just sit for a while, that's what the day is for. Nobody has to make a speech.

I know a lot of you are too far away to come, and I understand that completely. If you're in Boston or Perth or Leeds and can't make it, we'll take plenty of photographs and put them up here afterwards, and if anyone wants a video call on the day, tell me or tell Úna and we'll sort something out. I'll find someone who knows how to work the phone.

If you're thinking of coming, would you let me know by the end of November, just so I know how much soup to make. I'd rather have too much than run out.

**That's it**

That's everything, I think. The house is sold, the sale closes on the 15th of January, the reasons are above, and I've tried not to leave out the parts that don't make me look good. I'm sorry for how a lot of you found out about it. I'm not sorry about the decision itself, and I hope in time that'll make sense to those of you who are finding it hard.

Thank you for reading this far. I know it's long. Úna told me to keep it short and I didn't listen, which won't surprise her either.

I love you all, and I'll see as many of you as can make it on the 13th.

Mam / Nana / Auntie (whichever I am to you)
